newsitem.title: UK: Dollar boosted as Republican Congress tempers Clinton win.
newsitem.headline: Dollar boosted as Republican Congress tempers Clinton win.

text.p: Foreign exchange markets on Wednesday cheered the return of President Bill Clinton to the White House but were clearly relieved his hands, to some extent, will be tied by a Republican Congress.

"The markets are breathing a whole sigh of relief...Clinton has retained the White House and the Republicans have retained their grip on the House (of Representatives)," said David Brown, chief economist at Bear Stearns.
As European stock and bond markets climbed in the wake of the U.S. election results, the dollar moved up against the yen and mark.
"The result of the election has unleashed a big welter of buying. Not only on the forex side but also on the bond side," said Bear Stearn's Brown.
The dollar moved to a session high of 114.67 yen on Wednesday against 114.23 in late Europe on Tuesday while dollar/mark climbed to a session high of 1.5267 against 1.5200 in late Europe.

"Markets believe Clinton will keep a tight rein on the Republican tax cutting agenda, while the Republican Congress will operate to keep his spending priorities in check," Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank said.
As Clinton basked in the glory of a sweeping re-election on Wednesday, the Republicans easily held onto the Senate and clung on to control of the 435-seat House of Representatives.

While analysts are betting that Clinton's last term will herald a continuation of growth with low inflation, some fear the post election cheer could be short-lived and overshadowed by question marks over the strength of the dollar.
Ahead of the election the U.S. had a clear interest in a firm dollar policy to keep asset markets underpinned.
But some analysts fear that could change.
"(Treasury Secretary Robert) Rubin is the big architect of the strong dollar policy and if he were to leave that would leave a gap...And the markets would become nervous about that," said Fox.
But had the Democrats won the House of Representatives, pressure for a change in dollar policy would have been greater.
U.S. car makers have already sought to address the problem of the firmer dollar with the government.
"On the dollar side, you can be a bit nervous on the slant policy might take," Fox added.
"If the U.S. economy slows down and the auto-makers start to hit difficulty they will start to demand a softer dollar," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International.
